results.summary: The design covers the published Instagram core scope with dedicated services for social graph, posts, feed, stories, search, messaging, media storage, CDN delivery, and event-driven notifications, while explicitly addressing celebrity-scale feed handling and large media volume.

findings.title: Hybrid feed strategy matches both normal and celebrity authors
findings.explanation: The feed service explicitly combines fan-out-on-write for ordinary authors with fan-out-on-read for celebrity authors, which is the right architectural shape for the stated follower-scale constraint.

findings.title: Media delivery is separated from application traffic
findings.explanation: Direct uploads to object storage, background media processing, and CDN-based delivery keep large media bodies off the application servers and support the upload and feed paths cleanly.

findings.title: Event-driven downstream updates are consistently used
findings.explanation: Posts, stories, messages, and interactions publish committed events to a broker, and downstream consumers use those events for feed projection and notification delivery. That improves decoupling and retryability.

results.summary: The design covers all legacy core requirements with coherent service boundaries, event-driven fanout, direct media upload, cached personalized feeds, story expiry, search indexing, messaging, and notification delivery.

findings.title: Hybrid feed strategy for celebrity-scale accounts
findings.explanation: The feed service explicitly uses fan-out-on-write for ordinary authors and fan-out-on-read for celebrity authors, which is the right trade-off for handling accounts with millions of followers without overloading write amplification.

findings.title: Separated media, metadata, and delivery paths
findings.explanation: Media bytes are stored in object storage, metadata is kept in dedicated stores, and the CDN serves renditions near viewers. This clean separation supports scale and reduces unnecessary application-server load.

findings.title: Event-driven downstream processing
findings.explanation: Posts, stories, messages, and follow/interactions publish events to a broker, which cleanly decouples notifications and feed projection from the write paths.

results.summary: The design covers the full legacy Instagram scope with coherent paths for uploads, social graph, feed, stories, search, messaging, and notifications, while explicitly handling celebrity-scale feed delivery and media storage efficiency.

findings.title: Hybrid feed strategy addresses both normal and celebrity accounts
findings.explanation: The feed service combines fan-out-on-write for ordinary authors with fan-out-on-read for celebrity authors, which is the key architectural trade-off needed for the stated follower scale.

findings.title: Media upload path avoids routing large files through application servers
findings.explanation: Direct client-to-object-storage upload, plus asynchronous processing and CDN delivery, is a strong fit for high upload availability and media efficiency.

findings.title: Event-driven notifications and downstream projections are well separated
findings.explanation: Committed service events feed both feed projection and real-time notifications, which keeps write paths decoupled from read optimization and notification delivery.

results.summary: The design covers the full Instagram-style core scope with coherent services for uploads, social graph, posts, feed, stories, search, messaging, and notifications, and it addresses the published scale and latency constraints with appropriate async and caching strategies.

findings.title: Celebrity-aware feed fanout is a strong scalability choice
findings.explanation: The feed service explicitly switches between fan-out-on-write for ordinary authors and fan-out-on-read for celebrity accounts, which is a practical way to support extreme follower counts without overloading write paths.

findings.title: Direct uploads and asynchronous processing reduce availability risk
findings.explanation: Media uploads bypass application servers, write directly to object storage, and hand off processing to a worker, which keeps the upload path resilient and avoids tying upload availability to CPU-heavy media transforms.

findings.title: Explicit expiry handling for stories avoids TTL correctness dependence
findings.explanation: Stories are rejected based on expiresAt during reads, while TTL cleanup is relegated to storage reclamation, which preserves correctness even if deletion lags.

results.summary: The design cleanly covers the Instagram core scope with direct media upload, social graph, post interactions, feed generation, stories, search, messaging, notifications, and scale-aware storage and delivery paths.

findings.title: No material core gaps detected in the submitted architecture
findings.explanation: The submission covers the published core requirements with coherent service boundaries, storage separation for media, event-driven updates, and explicit handling for stories, search, messaging, feed generation, and celebrity-scale authors.

results.summary: The design cleanly places rate limiting at the gateway with shared Redis state, tiered versioned policy control, asynchronous telemetry, and multiple algorithm options, covering the published core scope well.

findings.title: No material core defects detected
findings.explanation: The submitted architecture covers the published core requirements and constraints with a coherent gateway-plus-shared-state design, including tiered policies, distributed enforcement, 429 responses, telemetry, and multiple algorithms.

results.summary: A coherent API rate limiter design with gateway-based enforcement, shared Redis decision state, versioned tier policies, multiple algorithm support, and asynchronous telemetry for monitoring and alerts.

findings.title: Default token bucket with policy-based algorithm selection
findings.explanation: The submitted rationale selects token bucket as the default because it is compact and supports burst-plus-sustained control, while preserving other algorithms through versioned policy selection. This is a strong fit for the brief's flexibility requirement.

findings.title: Shared Redis decision state keeps enforcement distributed and accurate
findings.explanation: Using an authoritative shard with atomic check-and-update centralizes correctness state without relying on instance affinity, which is a coherent strategy for distributed rate limiting and accurate counters.

findings.title: Asynchronous telemetry avoids adding latency to the request path
findings.explanation: The breach telemetry queue and downstream analytics/monitoring path are explicitly asynchronous, so operational visibility does not block admit/deny decisions.

results.summary: A coherent gateway-centered rate limiter with shared Redis state, versioned tier policies, asynchronous telemetry, and explicit support for multiple algorithms and distributed enforcement.

findings.title: Token-bucket default with policy-selected alternatives
findings.explanation: The design explicitly chooses token bucket as the default and preserves fixed-window, sliding-window, and leaky-bucket implementations behind versioned tier policy selection, which directly addresses the multi-algorithm constraint while keeping the common path compact.

findings.title: Distributed enforcement uses an authoritative shared state store
findings.explanation: Rate-limit decisions are made at the gateway against shared Redis state with atomic check-and-update, so limits remain consistent across gateway instances instead of being tied to local process memory or instance affinity.

findings.title: Observability path is isolated from request latency
findings.explanation: The gateway emits batched breach and health telemetry to a queue, which is then aggregated and monitored asynchronously. That gives alerting and operational visibility without blocking the admit/deny path.

findings.title: Per-tier policy management is explicitly versioned
findings.explanation: Policies are stored separately from hot counters, include tier and algorithm metadata, and are refreshed by the gateway from a bounded cache. This keeps operational policy changes manageable and decoupled from the request path.

results.summary: A coherent distributed rate limiter centered on a gateway, shared Redis state, versioned tier policies, and asynchronous telemetry/alerts, with clear 429 responses and multiple algorithm support.

findings.title: Shared-state gateway correctly centralizes enforcement
findings.explanation: The design keeps rate-limit correctness in the gateway plus Redis, rather than in the load balancer or application service, which preserves consistent enforcement across instances.

findings.title: Policy-driven multi-algorithm support is clearly represented
findings.explanation: The policy store and gateway explicitly support versioned tier policies and multiple algorithm choices, with token bucket as a sensible default and alternatives retained for boundary/precision tradeoffs.

findings.title: Asynchronous telemetry keeps alerting off the request path
findings.explanation: Breach events and health signals are buffered through a queue before aggregation and monitoring, so analytics and alert delivery do not add request-path latency.

results.summary: The design cleanly enforces distributed rate limits at the gateway with shared Redis state, versioned policy selection, actionable 429 responses, and asynchronous telemetry for monitoring.

findings.title: Asynchronous breach telemetry preserves request-path latency
findings.explanation: The design sends denials and health signals to a queue and only later aggregates them, which avoids coupling monitoring/alerting to the admission decision.

findings.title: Authoritative Redis decision path supports distributed correctness
findings.explanation: Using shared Redis state with atomic check-and-update on the authoritative shard is a strong fit for consistent rate limiting across many gateway instances.

findings.title: Policy-driven algorithm selection improves maintainability and flexibility
findings.explanation: Versioned policy storage plus a gateway-side algorithm selector cleanly separates policy from enforcement and makes it easy to support multiple algorithms.

results.summary: The design covers ingestion, typed aggregation, low-latency querying, alerting, dashboards, and historical retention with a coherent hot-store/archive split and burst-tolerant pipeline.

findings.title: Burst absorption and replay are explicitly designed
